entries.title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
entries.summary: Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia.Today,
entries.content:
Jeanette Manfra

VP, Head of Risk and Compliance, Google Cloud

Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia.

Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology.

To understand how existing technology environments shape an organization’s ability to operationalize AI, Google Cloud partnered with Hypothesis Group to survey 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The findings reveal a critical paradox: the legacy software systems enterprises rely on to deliver technology to their employees are simultaneously functioning as an innovation tax, actively holding back the AI transformation leaders are trying to achieve.

Legacy IT’s operational toll

In our study, we defined “legacy” technology as software running locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud. Across industries, decision-makers report that maintaining this footprint exerts a constant friction on their AI ambitions.

The consequences to AI are not theoretical. Nearly half (49%) of respondents report that relying on on-premises software has actively delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives.

Digging deeper, routine patch application and maintenance emerged as a primary operational bottleneck. As AI-enabled vulnerability discovery accelerates, the rate at which flaws are surfaced in legacy codebases has outpaced what human security teams can realistically address.

This creates a zero-sum game between routine maintenance of legacy systems and AI modernization. Instead of directing engineer cycles toward AI modernization, IT teams are spending their time and resources on maintaining legacy systems.

Enterprise monoculture

Customer choice

The solution to vendor lock-in is straightforward: enterprise buyers and policymakers must ensure organizations have genuine choice and interoperability in their software, cloud and AI architectures.

Furthermore, 80% of leaders agree that a provider’s installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, while 78% believe that the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. Organizations want the freedom to choose best-of-breed intelligence on its own merits, rather than accepting bundled defaults tied to legacy desktop software.

Accelerate agentic technology

Delivering this level of autonomous agility across the enterprise requires modern technology built to support the agentic era. Here are a few ideas to get there:

  • Demand architectural and provider choice: AI and cloud must never be held hostage by the legacy software running local servers, email or desktop operating systems. Organizations need the commercial and architectural freedom to select best-of-breed IT on its own merits.
  • Commit to secure-by-design foundations: The industry must move past the broken cycle of releasing insecure software and patching it after the fact. Software manufacturers must engineer durable, resilient architectures where entire vulnerability classes are eliminated before code ever ships — relieving understaffed IT teams from perpetual applying routine but necessary patches.
  • Deploy AI-driven defense to remediate legacy debt: For the millions of lines of vulnerable legacy software already running in production, organizations must shift from manual triage to proactive, AI-assisted defense. By deploying platforms like Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics, teams can use intelligence to continuously surface active exploit paths, prioritize critical exposure and automate remediation across complex, hybrid environments.

The promise of agentic AI is to help automate friction away, and accelerate human ingenuity. But that future cannot be built on top of software designed decades ago. As IT leaders plan their roadmaps, it is time to ask: Is your technology foundation accelerating your future, or are you paying a maintenance tax just to keep the past running?

Learn more about the research here.

entries.content:
Chris Betz

CISO, Google Cloud

Get original CISO insights in your inbox

The latest on security from Google Cloud's Office of the CISO, twice a month.

Subscribe

Welcome to the first Cloud CISO Perspectives for November 2026. Today, Chris Betz shares our security forecast for 2027, with insights from top leaders at Google, Google Cloud, and Mandiant.

As with all Cloud CISO Perspectives, the contents of this newsletter are posted to the Google Cloud blog. If you’re reading this on the website and you’d like to receive the email version, you can subscribe here.

Our security forecast for 2027

By Chris Betz, CISO, Google Cloud

Today, we’re publishing insights on the cybersecurity trends and challenges we anticipate in 2027, including agentic threats, changing attack tactics, and the new security defense approaches required.

This year we’ve witnessed a fundamental change in cybersecurity. When the year began, only a few organizations were using LLMs and agents to find and fix vulnerabilities. Today, it’s happening at scale across enterprises.

Organizations expected a reality with agentic hacking where scale, speed and sophistication would outpace human-only response; today, we’re seeing it in practice. Organizations predicted software development at an unheard of pace; today, we’re securing software delivered in hours and days instead of weeks and months.

We have passed many milestones, and the world won’t go back — and we are all digging in to fully understand the new reality.

The year ahead promises to be challenging, exciting, innovative and will outpace 2026. In the year ahead, enterprise software will change as agility and speed provided by agentic development shifts us from a collection of static applications to a live fabric of autonomous agents that can manage pricing, negotiate supplier contracts, allocate capital, and reroute supply chains in real time.

To make this vision a reality, many organizations are rushing to build agents. It’s on us as an industry to ensure the development and operations models are designed to be trustworthy and safe.

The risks in 2027 won’t be just server outages or stolen databases. As the agentic operations world takes off, we also need to be concerned about the data and technology foundation that agents rely on.

When an agent makes a consequential decision, you must be able to reconstruct the entire story: what inputs came in, how the agent reasoned through them, which tools it called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it. Without that trace, you can't debug it, you can't validate its correctness, and you can't trust it. And if you can't trust it, you can't scale it.

Karthik Narain, chief product and customer officer, Google Cloud

Security must evolve to protect the balance sheet through decision integrity. Every consequential action taken by an autonomous system requires a complete, tamper-proof decision trace, recording and tracking:

  • Inputs entered into the system.

  • How the model reasoned through its decisions.

  • Which tools the model called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it.

Collecting this data will help ensure that your teams can reconstruct, validate, and audit every automated decision before scaling.

Making the alert queue disappear, from chasing tickets to setting doctrine

For decades, security operations centers (SOCs) have suffered from crippling alert fatigue — too many alerts compounded by legacy security tools that hand human analysts half-finished investigations. When autonomous threats can probe a network and move laterally in minutes, human defenders can’t manually stitch together logs across eight different consoles or approve individual defensive actions at microsecond speed.

2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes.

Ramya Chitrakar, vice-president, Engineering, Google Cloud Security

That broken alert queue disappears in 2027 by flipping the operational model. The alert becomes the final output of an investigation. Autonomous defensive agents will handle the data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket.

Instead of chasing alerts at a keyboard, human analysts move up the stack to set strategic doctrine, define risk appetite, and verify automated actions built for rapid explainability — where any defensive decision can be understood by a human in 60 seconds and reversed in 30.

Moving Beyond Zero: Transaction-level trust and first-class agent identities

As enterprises deploy thousands of custom agents across multicloud environments, flat trust architectures, shared human service accounts, and blanket administrator tokens are turning internal workflows into high-leverage entry points for prompt injection and lateral movement.

Traditional Zero Trust is too rigid and broad to govern autonomous software acting on its own.

We need to extend the Zero Trust concept, not just at the network layer and the machine layer, but now down to the transaction layer.

Heather Adkins, vice-president, Security Engineering, Google

The year ahead demands an architectural shift to Beyond Zero so we can extend verification down to every individual transaction, network packet, and point-in-time authorization. Every autonomous agent should be treated as a first-class identity with its own verifiable credentials, strict least-privileged scope, and open communication standards. 

When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous.

Closing the loop between live runtime and defect-free code

The traditional divide between writing software and securing it is breaking down, while adversaries actively target the open-source libraries and external tools that coding assistants pull into codebases. Developers can no longer file a ticket and wait weeks for a manual security review, yet deploying hasty, unvalidated automated patches in production is just as dangerous to business continuity as the vulnerability itself.

Adversaries aren't just attacking model math and algorithms. They're actually poisoning the open source software, supply chain, MCP tools, and external libraries that agentic coding assistants pull automatically into code bases.

Sandra Joyce, vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence

In 2027, security becomes a closed-loop, continuous system embedded directly into the software delivery pipeline. By placing agentic reasoning inside developer tools, we can perform threat modeling and catch configuration errors side-by-side as code is written.

It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production.

Turning internal ground truth into a decisive defender advantage

Concerns persist around attackers gaining the upper hand in cybersecurity, and many fear autonomous capabilities will only widen that gap in 2027. Adversaries are already compressing six months of reconnaissance into hours, and exploiting flaws before vendors even know they exist. Compounding the challenge for defenders, no single model can discover or patch every vulnerability across code and cloud on its own.

The defender's advantage is that attackers operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork. Defenders own the complete ground truth, identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and real-time runtime activity.

Sandra Joyce, vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence

In the year ahead, defenders will use autonomous technology to capitalize on the one thing an outside attacker will never have: complete internal ground truth. While adversaries operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork, defenders own the full picture of their identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and live runtime activity.

By feeding that unified context into multi-model ensembles — such as pairing lightweight models for continuous scanning with deep reasoning models that cross-validate findings and eliminate false positives — organizations can spot and remediate toxic combinations of permissions and configurations that look harmless in isolation, before an external attacker can ever piece them together.

Countering asymmetric threat speed and the new extortion playbook

Not every adversary will embrace machine speed the same way in 2027. While state-sponsored espionage actors often avoid loud, hyper-fast automated scripts that risk triggering alarms and blowing their long-term stealth, cybercriminals tend to go all-in on autonomous velocity.

What we're seeing right now is a variety of adversaries that are exploiting vulnerabilities before the vendors even know about it.

Charles Carmakal, CTO, Mandiant Consulting

As endpoint defenses get better at blocking traditional file-encrypting ransomware, criminal crews are shifting to rapid, high-volume data theft and extortion — specifically targeting proprietary model weights, custom agent skills, prompt libraries, and cloud GPU compute (“LLMJacking”).

Preparation here means eliminating security silos. It’s a critical failure point to treat models, agent permissions, software supply chains, and cloud infrastructure as separate domains.

Instead, we want to unite them under a single, intelligence-led governance framework that allows defenders to lock down high-value autonomous assets and shut down extortion paths before data can leave the environment.

Red-teaming the agentic enterprise before adversaries attack

In the rush to capture productivity gains in the year ahead, many enterprises are deploying custom agents directly into core business workflows without testing how those systems behave under adversarial pressure. That mistake leaves guardrails vulnerable to bypasses, scanner blinding, and indirect prompt injection.

One of the things that the team's been doing over the past few years is doing a lot of red team exercises… with those agentic solutions, so that we have the opportunity to identify and fix the issues before an adversary has the ability to do that against victim organizations.

Charles Carmakal, CTO, Mandiant Consulting

Continuous, proactive adversarial red-teaming must be a mandatory prerequisite before any autonomous workflow touches production. Systematically attempting to break into agentic systems, bypass safety controls, and manipulate model behavior prior to deployment is crucial to securing the agentic era.

Critically, model safety engineering should combine the results of those tests with frontline threat intelligence on novel attack prompts and evasion techniques. Defenders can then harden classifiers and neutralize new attack techniques before adversaries can use them against real victims.

Orchestrating specialized agent teams to prevent agent sprawl

Relying on a single generalist agent to defend an enterprise will fail in 2027 because deep technical skills do not transfer across domains. For example, an agent built to reverse-engineer malware is not the agent that should reason about an identity blast radius.

As departments across the business rapidly spin up uncoordinated, standalone agents without centralized oversight, agent sprawl is emerging as the next iteration of shadow IT, threatening to derail enterprise agent deployments through inadequate governance.

Technological adoption cannot outpace architectural governance… We have to prioritize machine speed defense. Security cannot remain a manual checkpoint that slows innovation down.

Sandra Joyce, vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence

Just as a well-coordinated human team beats a lone generalist, the year ahead belongs to orchestrated networks of specialized hunter, decoder, and responder agents, each operating with its own domain depth, memory, and dedicated tools.

Succeeding at scale requires building the governance and orchestration layer first. The key here will be to establish graduated autonomy, shared state, clean handoffs between specialized agents, and a central coordinator that knows precisely when to act autonomously and when to escalate to a human.

To learn more about our cybersecurity guidance for the coming year, check out our Security 2027 video.

In case you missed it

Here are the latest updates, products, services, and resources from our security teams so far this month:

  • Helping you build and defend at machine-speed in the agentic era: At Security Summit 2026, we are sharing updates on how organizations can build securely, secure systems, and defend at machine speed in the agentic era. Read more.

  • How Google Does It: Using agents to help find, track, and fix vulnerabilities: Threat actors can now find software flaws faster than ever. To maintain an agile, responsive defense, we now use agentic systems with existing foundations. Read more.

  • How to use agents to stop insider threats: As agents find their place across the enterprise, we want to be sure that they neither become an insider threat nor enable people to become one. Read more.

  • Empowering SOC teams with the Wiz Red and Blue agents: Red Agent gives SOC teams validated pre-breach alerts, while Blue Agent investigates active threats at machine speed, helping teams stay ahead in the AI threat era. Read more.

  • The ROI of agentic remediation with Wiz Green Agent: Learn how Fireblocks, Rogo, and project44 used Green Agent to eliminate cross-team blockers and accelerate critical risk resolution. Read more.

  • Responding to core PHP vulnerabilities CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-10961: Follow these recommendations to minimize remote code execution risks in PHP from two critical vulnerabilities in the core PHP language runtime. Read more.

  • Working collaboratively to fight scams in Asia Pacific: To help tackle scams in the Asia Pacific region, here’s how we combine built-in protections, local partnerships, and education. Read more.

Please visit the Google Cloud blog for more security stories published this month.

Threat Intelligence news

  • The rise of LLMJacking: How threat actors monetize compromised resources: Mandiant responded to multiple incidents in 2026 in which threat actors hijacked enterprise access to large language models, a tactic known as LLMJacking that can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours. Read more.

  • Shutting the door on the XCPE botnet: Google and industry partners dismantled the XCPE backdoor that had assembled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes into a botnet. We assessed with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Company, an Android original equipment manufacturer and original design manufacturer. Read more.

  • ARTEX and friends: Enter agentic offensive frameworks: Since September, Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant have observed multiple threat actors abusing the open-source, agentic pentesting frameworks ARTEX, Hexstrike, and CAIRN to conduct a broad range of actions across multiple phases of the attack life cycle. Read more.

  • Investigating ephemeral supply chain tampering: For the first time, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant have encountered a software supply chain compromise that was implemented with very short tampering windows that were active for only five to 10 minutes, and effectively evading traditional point-in-time triage and automated file scanning. Read more.

Please visit the Google Cloud blog for more threat intelligence stories published this month.

entries.title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
entries.summary: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers
entries.content:
Fenghui Zhang

Distinguished Engineer, Google Cloud

Weiren Yu

Senior Product Manager, Google Cloud

As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle.

We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation.

For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync.

Across this shared model-state layer, TPU Sync integrates directly into existing infrastructure stacks across PyTorch (via TorchTPU) and JAX — serving as the TPU KV cache connector for vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d disaggregated serving, while providing low-level transfer primitives for Pathways and multi-controller JAX (McJAX) RL pipelines.

Understanding TPU Sync: The kitchen analogy

To understand TPU Sync’s impact, imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen. Think of the TPU as an incredibly fast executive chef working on a tiny countertop (the chip's HBM). When preparing a massive feast, the chef needs lots of ingredients (the KV cache), which quickly clutter the counter.

  • The standard kitchen (without TPU Sync): When the small counter fills up, the chef has to toss out prepped ingredients and chop them again from scratch the next time an order needs them — stalling the kitchen on repetitive prep work (prefill recomputation).

  • The upgraded kitchen (with TPU Sync): TPU Sync adds a spacious side pantry (pinned host RAM), a shared walk-in cold storage room accessible to every station in the kitchen (shared cluster storage), and a coordinated team of runners. The runners slide full prep trays directly between the counter, the pantry, and peer stations without repacking them (direct DMA in native TPU layout).

Crucially, the runners swap trays in and out while the chef keeps cooking (asynchronous, non-blocking transfers).

Key use cases for TPU Sync

TPU Sync improves system throughput and latency in workloads requiring deep context, high concurrency, multi-turn reasoning and RL rollouts:

  • Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats: When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage).

  • Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation.

  • Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead.

  • Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates.

Breaking through the memory wall with TPU Sync

At its core, TPU Sync establishes a high-performance data transfer path between TPU HBM and host RAM, as well as across TPU hosts via the DCN. It achieves this through four key architectural advantages:

  • Layout-preserving direct DMA with in-place buffer aliasing: TPU Sync accesses the underlying JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place and moves slices directly between TPU HBM and page-locked (

    DmaMap
    -registered) host memory in a single hardware DMA. By keeping tensors in their native TPU physical tile layout across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and the wire, data lands ready for immediate Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) execution with no Python serialization, no layout conversion, and no user-space bounce buffers.

  • Compute-overlapped transfers: Rather than taking an exclusive lock or making an on-device copy of static KV cache and weight buffers, TPU Sync creates raw PJRT buffer aliases (

    PJRT_RawBuffer
    ) without holding PJRT usage locks so block-level transfers can run concurrently with active in-place computation, with built-in DMA pacing to keep large transfers from delaying kernel launches.

  • No XLA compilation in the data path: Because TPU Sync executes transfers and tile-aware strided resharding in native C++ outside the XLA graph, moving KV blocks or resharding weights across different trainer and sampler topologies does not trigger runtime compilation — keeping the data path fast and framework-agnostic.

  • High-bandwidth PCIe DMA and DCN streaming: Using the 

    raw_transfer
    library’s direct PJRT raw-buffer DMA pipeline, TPU Sync reaches up to 223 GB/s of aggregate D2H and H2D throughput per Ironwood (TPU v7x) host out of the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 hardware ceiling, and streams across the DCN at up to ~192 Gbps on a single 200 Gbps NIC (or ~350 Gbps across dual 200 Gbps NICs with NUMA-aware multi-NIC striping).

TPU Sync exposes a low-level data transfer API, making it easier for developers to integrate high-speed TPU data transfer into higher-level frameworks.

Higher-level architecture

Built on top of its core transport and resharding primitives, TPU Sync provides a modular orchestration stack for distributed cache management:

  • Global KV store: A global registry that maps prompt prefix hashes to physical cache blocks, handles dynamic lookups, and coordinates LRU eviction and tier demotion.

  • TPU Sync controller: The orchestration layer that generates transfer plans, coordinates data movement across nodes, and handles lease management and recovery.

  • KV cache manager: The local execution engine that tracks block states, manages HBM, host DRAM (including 

    /dev/shm
    warm-boot persistence) alongside experimental POSIX storage backends, and executes asynchronous DMA transfers.

Figure 1. TPU Sync operates as the model-state layer on TPU, unifying TPU HBM (Tier 1), pinned host DRAM (Tier 2), shared storage (Tier 3), and multi-host DCN under a single layout-preserving DMA data plane.

Solving disaggregated serving and prefix caching

Let us take a closer look at how TPU Sync helps with some of the use cases we listed in the earlier section. By treating host pinned memory as a substantial, high-speed Tier 2 cache, TPU Sync reduces the fragmentation and memory limits of standard HBM setups.

Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregated serving

In state-of-the-art serving topologies, prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases are isolated on separate node pools. To prevent latency bubbles, TPU Sync bridges this gap with a highly optimized, three-step pipeline:

  • Direct-DMA offloading: Once a prefill node processes an initial prompt, TPU Sync immediately moves the resulting KV blocks into pinned host RAM via its asynchronous D2H DMA path.

  • Host-to-host streaming: The TPU Sync controller then orchestrates a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) transfer, streaming the context directly to the assigned decode node.

  • Overlapped ingestion: As blocks arrive in the decode node's host RAM, TPU Sync triggers an asynchronous H2D transfer directly into TPU HBM. This happens concurrently with active decoding computation, substantially minimizing TTFT.

Host-powered prefix caching

For highly concurrent systems sharing large system prompts or running multi-turn agentic loops, TPU HBM is not large enough to hold multiple active cache blocks. TPU Sync extends the prefix cache out of HBM (Tier 1) into substantial, distributed host RAM pools (Tier 2). Because TPU Sync transfers are asynchronous, it overlaps the PCIe DMA loading of the next required prefix from host RAM with the compute of the current request — minimizing TPU idle time between requests.

For workloads that exceed even host DRAM capacity, TPU Sync also includes an experimental POSIX storage backend (Tier 3+) that asynchronously spills older KV blocks to local SSDs or shared Google Cloud Managed Lustre storage — pairing with llm-d prefix-affinity routing on GKE so replicas can recall cached prefixes across tiers without recomputing prompts.

Sample performance results

P/D disaggregated inference result highlights:

  • Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut: For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms.

  • Substantial TTFT reduction: Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency.

  • Substantial high-traffic scalability: During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution.

Prefix caching result highlights:

  • Expands KV cache capacity beyond HBM: When heavyweight MoE model weights consume most of device HBM, on-chip memory can hold only a few long-context prefixes. Offloading into pinned host DRAM expands effective cache capacity by an order of magnitude.

  • Sustains high cache-hit rates under concurrency: Pooling distributed host RAM keeps shared system prompts and multi-turn agent contexts warm across thousands of concurrent sessions instead of thrashing HBM.

  • Significantly reduces prefill recompute: Directly bypasses heavy compute layers for repeated instruction blocks and system prompts, reducing average TTFT by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads while delivering over 50% higher throughput and a 30% reduction in P99 inter-token latency (ITL).

Ecosystem adoption and partnerships

TPU Sync serves as the open, composable memory substrate across our PyTorch-on-TPU and Kubernetes serving ecosystem, built in close collaboration with key open-source maintainers and infrastructure partners:

  • Inferact (vLLM-TorchTPU): Co-engineered with Inferact, maintainers of vLLM-TorchTPU, TPU Sync is integrated directly via vLLM's native KVConnector interface. It powers Direct-DMA host DRAM offloading and multi-host P/D disaggregation across frontier open-source models.

  • llm-d 1.0 integration: llm-d 1.0 pairs with TPU Sync on GKE to deliver global prefix-cache-affinity routing, per-rank decode session pinning, and experimental two-stage capacity spill to Google Cloud Managed Lustre.
